 Trump: Actually, election security is a bad thing 
 by Lisa Needham 
 Staff 
 Tuesday, October 20, 2026 at 6:30 AM PDT

 Signs point to the entrance on the last day of early voting before the 2022 midterms. AP 
 Back when we had a functioning government, we also had a functioning Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and it worked directly with state election officials to secure voting infrastructure against things like, say, Russian cyberattacks .
 But CISA was always going to end up in President Donald Trump’s crosshairs for many reasons.
 First, Trump’s first-term CISA Director Christopher Krebs ran afoul of Trump because he dared to say—correctly—that the 2020 election was the “most secure in American history.”
 Former CISA Director Christopher Krebs AP 
 Trump fired Krebs in 2021 and then issued one of his unhinged executive orders in 2025 titled, “Addressing Risks from Chris Krebs and Government Censorship.” 
 Great, terrific, not dystopian at all.
 Next, CISA’s actual remit included things like calling out Russian disinformation election efforts, but that’s not cool with Trump either because he will never admit that Russia regularly interferes in U.S. elections, putting its thumb on the scale for Trump and the GOP. 
 Trump remains incandescently furious that his 2016 win was perhaps brought about in part by that same type of Russian “help.”
 See, in Trump’s topsy-turvy world, actually securing elections against Russian interference is bad. CISA should instead be helping him rewrite the history of the 2020 election and assisting the federal government  take over elections—despite that pesky Constitution leaving them to the states.
 But now that the administration has gutted CISA’s funding and staff, what’s left for it to do?
 Apparently, CISA was supposed to secretly hack election machines and report their findings to the White House.
 Wait, what?
 Related | Democrats change up voting plans to avoid Trump’s mail meddling 
 CISA’s whole deal is sort of the opposite of this, what with being the ones who are supposed to thwart election-machine hacking. 
 You can tell exactly how sincere an effort at actual election security this was by this little fact: CISA was instructed, if it found any actual flaws, not to inform the voting-machine companies.
 “My thought was they could keep it in their back pocket to invalidate any [election] results they don’t like,” an unnamed former CISA official told ProPublica.
 Exactly that. 
 What the administration is looking for here is not election security, but a way to manipulate elections to come out favorably for the GOP—because it knows full well that Republicans can’t win on merits. 
 Clay Bennett/Tribune Content Agency 
 CISA employees had to explain over and over again to whatever nightmare political appointees Trump put atop their agency that this wasn’t possible—in part because the people who were capable of this sort of hacking were laid off during the so-called Department of Government Efficiency’s purge.
 Where CISA used to work in collaboration with the states, advising them on cybersecurity needs, it’s now just another part of Trump’s push to wreck elections. 
 “Our number one risk at this point is the federal government,” Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold told Politico.
 And she’s not wrong. Trump is engaged in a full-scale assault on election integrity, spinning up long-debunked conspiracy theories and whipping up a panic about nonexistent immigrant voter fraud.
 States are struggling to hold their elections together in the face of this onslaught. Congress could—and should—stop it, since the Constitution gives only that branch the power to alter election rules. But the GOP majorities in both chambers have decided to cede all authority to Trump. 
 That’ll change come Jan. 3, 2027—and the administration isn’t going to like it at all.
